PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Run — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches running as a whole-body team: arms pump with the legs, feet land light, eyes look ahead — and stopping on the word is part of the sport.

What is this?

Run is fast travel on foot: arms bent and pumping opposite the legs, feet landing light and quick, eyes ahead — and a good runner can STOP when the word comes.

What does it mean?

Children run for joy before they run for sport — the teaching gift is the teamwork story (arms help legs!) and the stop-skill: a runner who can stop on command is safe on every playground and street.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three run ideas: the arms PUMP, bent at the elbows, opposite to the legs — pumping arms lift the run; light feet — quiet quick steps, not thunder stomps; and the stop is trained — one word, feet plant, body brakes.

Why this matters

Running is the wall’s most-used skill — every chase, every race, every game of tag — and arm-pump plus stop-on-word turns joyful chaos into actual sport.

What it teaches

Arm-leg opposition (a real coordination milestone), light-landing gait, stopping control, and the joy of open sprinting.

Words to learn

runarms pumplight feetsprintstopfinish linefast

Say this to your child

“"Running is arms-and-legs teamwork! Pump your arms, bent elbows, opposite to your legs — feel the lift? Land light like a quiet fox — quick steps, no thunder. And a good runner can STOP: one word, feet plant, statue! Arms pump, feet light, stop on the word — now race me to the tree!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is run — fast feet and pumping arms!"
  2. The arms: elbows bent, fists soft, pump them opposite the legs — walk slowly while pumping to feel the teamwork.
  3. The light feet: run like a quiet fox — quick light steps. Thunder-stomps slow you down; light feet fly.
  4. The stop: practise "run… STOP!" — feet plant, body brakes, statue. Three stops without toppling wins the badge.
  5. Play the run games below and close: "arms pump, feet light, stop on the word."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Run" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly running illustration below — exactly as the pumping arms look.

Ask your child

"What do the arms do? What do quiet fox feet sound like? What happens on the word STOP?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Arms pump opposite!" "Light feet — quiet fox!" or the braked one: "STOP — statue, no topple!"

Out in the real world

Runs fill every playground, garden and hallway (carefully!) — and the arm-pump is visible on every sprinter on screen: watch a race and find the teamwork. The stop skill is the street-crossing skill too.

Try it together

Line Races + Stop Badge: two chalk lines, sprint between them with pumping arms and light feet — race after race, joy first. Then the Stop Badge round: run freely until the call — "STOP!" — plant and statue; three clean stops earn the stop badge (any sticker). Finish with a lap of honour, arms pumping. Fast feet, fox steps, trustworthy brakes.

Understanding check

Ask: "What pumps opposite the legs? What do light feet sound like? What is the stop skill for?" The arms, a quiet fox, safety — three answers and the race is on.

Parent tips

Walk-and-pump first for the arm-leg opposition — slow motion teaches the pattern. And never call STOP mid-stride of the youngest runner: call it on the landing beat.

This lesson pairs with the Run flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.
